newsitem.title: USA: Curtain set to rise on new era at old MGM.
newsitem.headline: Curtain set to rise on new era at old MGM.

text.p: The curtain will rise on a new era for one of Hollywood's oldest movie studios on Thursday when a group led by billionaire Kirk Kerkorian closes its $1.3 billion acquisition of Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Inc.

The new owners, Kerkorian's Tracinda Corp. and Australian media company Seven Network Ltd., face the immediate challenge of kick starting production with $350 million in working capital -- about half what experts say is needed.
"Obviously, (that number) puts you at a disadvantage to a Warner Bros or Buena Vista," said Arthur Rockwell of Los Angeles-based Yaeger Capital Management. "But that's life when you're re-starting."
Warner Bros., the studio unit of Time Warner Inc. and Walt Disney Co.'s Buena Vista unit are both well-established film operations.

MGM's new owners take the reins just after a key executive, John Calley, plans to leave his post as head of MGM's United Artists film unit to take over Sony Corp.'s troubled Sony Pictures Entertainment unit.

Industry insiders believe the loss of Calley is not critical to the studio's long-term success, but they say MGM Chairman Frank Mancuso must act quickly to name a replacement to avoid any more gaps in film production.
The nearly year-long sale already curtailed MGM's film slate for late 1996 and the first half of 1997 because studio executives were unable to close deals and start production.

As a result, MGM will have only one to two movies out for the Christmas season and will very likely miss the crucial late spring and summer box office seasons. A full distribution schedule won't resume until 1997's third quarter, a studio spokeswoman said.

Sources close to the studio believe it will make about $75 million in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization for 1996. That number is expected to fall, however, in 1997 to about $55 million.
Officials for the new MGM ownership team declined to comment on future cash flow.
Beyond 1997, the new owners see a tremendous synergy between the film studio and MGM Grand Inc., the huge Las Vegas casino that is majority-owned by Kerkorian.

Last week at an investor conference in Las Vegas MGM's casino management, which bills the MGM Grand as a "City of Entertainment" based on MGM movies, was trumpeting the ability to hold film premieres in Las Vegas and possibly building casinos themed around the James Bond movies.
Also, the overseas investment of Seven Network gives MGM muscle in the Asia Pacific region where it is already starting up a cable television network called MGM Gold Networks.
The studio, founded in 1924, has produced some of the film industry's most acclaimed movies and enduring characters, such as "West Side Story", "Raging Bull" and 17 James Bond films.

But it fell on hard times after being acquired in 1990 by Italian financier Giancarlo Paretti, and eventually slipped into bankruptcy. Only in 1996 has its trademark "Leo the Lion" re-charged its world famous roar with films like "Goldeneye", "The Birdcage" and "Leaving Las Vegas."
